concepts.definition: Active intermediary placement between communicating peers.
concepts.failureExample: A service accepts an attacker-provided certificate during TLS setup.

concepts.decision: Reduce credential exposure, separate privilege, segment, monitor, and remediate artifacts and sessions.
concepts.definition: Use of captured password-derived authentication material without knowing the original password.
concepts.failureExample: An attacker reuses a captured hash against reachable hosts.
concepts.label: Pass The Hash

concepts.decision: Review ticket issuance, service identity, delegation, encryption/signing choices, and endpoint compromise.
concepts.definition: Ticket-based authentication system whose security depends on identity, service account, delegation, time, and directory controls.
concepts.failureExample: A stale privileged service account has broad delegation rights.
concepts.label: Kerberos

concepts.decision: Prepare protected backups, incident authority, containment, recovery testing, and restored-system validation.
concepts.definition: Availability and business-impact attack involving encryption, extortion, exfiltration, or disruption.
concepts.failureExample: A backup exists but is deleted through the compromised administrator’s account.
concepts.label: Ransomware

concepts.decision: Protect collection, storage, endpoints, logs, privileged workflows, and response processes.
concepts.definition: Acquisition of passwords, tokens, hashes, keys, tickets, or session material for unauthorized use.
concepts.failureExample: A diagnostic log records reusable access tokens.
concepts.label: Credential Theft

concepts.decision: Validate identity, trust anchor, version, parameters, freshness, and failure behavior.
concepts.definition: Authenticated and protected communication path with validated peers and safe negotiation.
concepts.failureExample: Traffic is encrypted but the client ignores the hostname mismatch.
concepts.label: Secure Channel

concepts.decision: Use when each endpoint or service must establish the other’s identity.
concepts.definition: Both parties verify the other before relying on the exchange.
concepts.failureExample: A client authenticates to a server that never proves it is the intended service.
concepts.label: Mutual Authentication

concepts.decision: Use to limit credential abuse, ransomware movement, and access to privileged paths.
concepts.definition: Restriction of reachability across network or system zones.
concepts.failureExample: A compromised workstation reaches backup administration directly.
concepts.label: Segmentation

concepts.decision: Protect backup identities, integrity, isolation, restore time, and post-restore validation.
concepts.definition: Protected, tested ability to restore required service and data after disruption.
concepts.failureExample: A backup completes successfully but has never been restored within the business deadline.
concepts.label: Backup Recovery

concepts.decision: Use unique identities, strong authentication, least privilege, monitoring, and emergency controls.
concepts.definition: Attributable, constrained management of high-authority accounts.
concepts.failureExample: A shared admin account encrypts production and deletes backups without attribution.
concepts.label: Privileged Account Management

misconceptions.claim: A current backup alone solves ransomware.
misconceptions.correction: Recovery also requires protected backup access, known-good systems, prioritization, restoration testing, credential containment, integrity validation, and business and security acceptance.

outcome: Analyze intermediary, pass-the-hash, Kerberos, and ransomware paths as protocol, credential, endpoint, authorization, monitoring, or recovery problems.

sections.body: A man-in-the-middle attacker attempts to position between communicating parties to observe, alter, relay, or influence the exchange. Secure channels need authenticated peers, correct certificate or key validation, fresh session behavior, protected negotiation, and resistance to downgrade or insecure fallback. Network encryption without endpoint validation can still permit an active intermediary. Evaluate trust anchors, names or identities, protocol versions, error behavior, session handling, and user or service decisions that accept untrusted prompts.
keyPoints: Confidential transport without peer authentication may not prevent active interception.
Negotiation and fallback paths are security-critical protocol behavior.
sections.title: Protect protocol negotiation and peer identity

sections.body: Pass-the-hash uses a captured password-derived credential artifact in authentication flows that accept it; changing a password alone may not remediate a stolen usable artifact until affected sessions and endpoints are addressed. Kerberos exploitation concerns identities, ticket issuance, service accounts, delegation, time, encryption or signing choices, directory authority, and endpoint compromise. Reduce exposure with least privilege, privileged-access separation, protected credential handling, strong authentication, service-account governance, patch and configuration management, segmentation, monitoring, and a tested credential-compromise response.
keyPoints: Credential theft is often an endpoint and privilege-management problem as well as an authentication problem.
A protocol weakness hypothesis must be checked against actual configuration and attacker access.
sections.title: Treat credential artifacts and ticket paths as privileged assets

sections.body: Ransomware can use initial access, credential abuse, privilege escalation, lateral movement, destructive encryption, exfiltration, and pressure on business operations. Layer prevention with segmentation, least privilege, hardened administration, protected backups, monitoring, incident response, and recovery rehearsals. Backup existence alone is insufficient: protect backup identities and paths, verify integrity and restore time, isolate or make recovery material resilient to the attacker’s privileges, and validate that restored systems are secure before returning to service. Preserve evidence and coordinate legal, business, and recovery authority.
keyPoints: Ransomware resilience is an architecture, operations, and continuity capability.
A fast restore from compromised identity or configuration can reinfect the environment.
sections.title: Contain impact and restore trustworthy operation

teaching.focalRelation: Peer validation and mutual authentication constrain intermediary paths; credential artifacts enable actions until contained; segmentation limits propagation; backup recovery restores data only when identities, systems, configurations, and integrity are known good.

learningJob.plainExplanation: Clean backups do not make compromised administrator identities trustworthy. Contain and replace credentials and sessions, protect the recovery plane, restore known-good systems, and obtain security and business acceptance.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: The containment-to-restoration chain adds ordering and recontamination risk, but it does not visually cover every intermediary, ticket, credential, and ransomware path promised by the broad title.
